entries:
Enhanced form of earlier bezichten (15th c.), denominal from now obsolete Bezicht (“accusation”), from Middle High German beziht, itself deverbal from Old High German bezīhan. Modern German bezeihen was gradually displaced, but is still attested until the early 20th century.
The form with -ig- (16th c.) appears to be of northern origin; compare Middle Low German betichtigen (14th c.), Middle Dutch betichtigen (early 15th c., though now only betichten). It follows the adjective in Middle Low German betichtich, Middle High German bezihtec (“accused, infamous”).

entries: Formally continuing Middle High German verītelen (“to become weak, insipid”, a 14th-c. hapax). By surface analysis, eitel (“vain”) + ver- -en. In Early Modern German, it is attested for “to empty, deplete”. The contemporary sense has been in use since the 18th c. While it can easily be explained from the underlying adjective, it should be noted that the same sense was well established in Middle Dutch already by the 15th c., so influence by Dutch verijdelen is possible.
